1:
The text itself is the first question. Lightfoot argues that Christ certainly said righteousness, but that common people could understand the word only of alms, the traditions having taught that alms conferred much toward justification; and that Matthew could not change in Greek where the Saviour had not changed in Syriac. Ellicott says the better manuscripts give righteousness, the wider word branching afterwards into alms, fasting and prayer, and thinks the narrower reading arose from a misconception; Robertson agrees, counting the three specimens that follow. Gill allows the reading and narrows it again, nothing being commoner among the Jews than to call alms righteousness, and Henry notes that they called the poor's box the box of righteousness. Calvin alone dismisses the question as of little moment.

The Gloss observes that Christ, having fulfilled the law in its commandments, now fulfils it in its promises, forbidding the two things Deuteronomy 28 held out — human glory and abundance of goods. Pseudo-Chrysostom sets the three duties against the three temptations — alms scattering what covetousness heaps, fasting against gluttony, prayer against the false glory assailed on the temple — vainglory alone among vices coming out of good. Chrysostom calls the desire of fame near akin to virtue, a beast hard to discern which enters secretly and carries off all within; John Chrysostom explains why the warning comes here and not earlier: the disease arises precisely when many commandments have been kept, so virtue had first to be implanted and the passion that mars its fruit purged after. Henry calls it the dead fly that spoils the whole box of ointment.

The fault, all insist, is in the motive and not the publicity. Ellicott puts it best: the disciple's ideal is to let his light shine before men, in the self-same words used at Matthew 5:16, and yet be indifferent to their praise; in most men the two motives mingle, and we dare not say at what stage the lower overpowers the higher. Barnes says we are not forbidden to give before men but to give in order to be seen. Pseudo-Chrysostom notices that the addition matters — not do not before men but to be seen of them — and that you deceive the very man whose good word you seek, since he supposes you did it for God. Augustine says none knows the strength of the love of glory but the man who has declared war on it: easy not to wish for praise when denied, hard not to be pleased when offered. He defends Paul, who both refuses to please men and pleases all men, as a traveller seeking a ship seeks not the ship but his country. Gregory allows only the perfect to let their deeds be seen without secret exultation.

The trumpet is the chapter's first real crux. Lightfoot says he has sought much and found no mention of a trumpet in almsgiving; Calvin says the same from history, treating it as the figure many languages use for ostentation beyond bounds; Ellicott sets out the two conjectures — a literal trumpet to summon the poor, or the clang of coin in the trumpet-shaped alms-chests — and rejects both, the first for want of evidence, the second as too weak for so active a verb. Clarke will not give up the literal sense, citing Harmer on dervishes who blow horns when anything is given them, and the rabbinic name for the alms-chest holes into which an ostentatious man might fling his money with a jingle. Robertson reports a missionary's testimony that Hindu priests do this very thing to gather a crowd, and concludes the rabbis could too. Robertson finds in the closing verb the papyrus term for a receipt in full — they can sign for their reward — which Henry turns into a threat: it is a reward, but their own, and a present one.
3:
The saying is taken as proverbial by Barnes, Wesley and Ellicott, a free hyperbole for extremest secrecy, though several look for something behind it. Lightfoot recalls that in certain religious acts the left hand was not allowed to meet the right — the sabbath cup taken with the right alone, the sacrificial blood neither received nor sprinkled with the left — and that Shammai fed himself with one hand only. Ellicott and Henry both suspect a reference to the right hand used in offering at the altar, Henry adding that the poor man's chest stood at the right of the temple passage, and Gill that the allusion is to the secret chamber where money was brought privately for the poor. Chrysostom presses it further: if it were possible you should not know yourself, and your very hands be hidden from your sight, that is what you should strive after — and if you want spectators you have angels and the God of the universe.

Augustine clears away two readings first. If the left hand means our enemy, why did the Lord heal with the Jews standing round, and how are we to feed an enemy who hungers? And the reading that makes it the wife, from whom a husband's charities should be hidden to avoid domestic strife, he calls ridiculous: the command is addressed to women too, and no theft is to be committed to do God service. Clarke keeps a modest version of the first sense, that charity must sometimes be hidden from relatives who would hinder it, and then from ourselves by our not eyeing it with complacency; Henry says the left hand is part of ourselves, and that adoring our own shadow is a branch of pride as dangerous as ostentation, citing Cicero that we should be moved by the object and not the observer. Ellicott offers a symbolic afterthought, that the right hand is the higher element which prompts true charity and the left the baser and self-seeking, between which a barrier should be set to exclude that mingling of motives which is at least the beginning of evil.

The promise divides them, because its last word is disputed. Robertson says flatly that openly was added by the received text here and at the sixth verse and is not genuine, since Jesus does not promise a reward for private piety; Ellicott agrees and calls it a curious early attempt to improve on our Lord's teaching, whether from a rhetorical taste wanting a completer antithesis or from the craving for public acknowledgment asserting itself even here, and holds that the addition lowers the truth, the reward being possibly immediate and secret. Clarke expounds the word as it stands, of substance increased and the witness of the Spirit in the heart; Calvin makes the reward wait for the last day, when what is now buried in darkness shall be revealed, and guards the passage against the objection that Scripture elsewhere commands us to edify by example, since Christ condemned ostentation and not doing good before men.
5:
The practice is documented before it is judged. Lightfoot shows from the rabbis that to stand was simply to pray, Maimonides requiring that a man stand, turn toward Jerusalem, cover his head and fix his eyes downward. Henry allows the posture but thinks kneeling humbler, so that standing savoured of self-confidence, and notes that the broad streets were chosen where two ways met, so every passer-by would see and hear; the Gloss says the same of the four cross-ways. Ellicott insists there was nothing ostentatious in the attitude itself, and locates the fault elsewhere: in going into the synagogue for private devotion, standing apart as if absorbed while secretly watching the impression made, and in reciting the eighteen benedictions in the open places with the veil of prayer over the head. Barnes and Wesley insist the word cannot mean the house of worship, since our Lord did not condemn prayer in synagogues.

Whether the closet is a room or a figure is the chapter's sharpest patristic disagreement. Barnes describes the actual chamber, raised a storey over the porch of every Jewish house — the upper room of the New Testament; Robertson gives the word as a store-house or private apartment; Ellicott renders it the store-closet and calls the rule a paradox that cannot bind literally, the place named being the one men would think it irreverent to connect with prayer. Augustine takes it otherwise: by our chambers understand our hearts, and the door is the bodily senses, to be shut against the worldly things and the crowd of vain imaginings that beset us in prayer. Calvin refuses that outright: expositors give it an allegorical turn, but there is no necessity for such trifling. We are commanded in many places to pray in the public assembly, and Christ does not withdraw us from it; he speaks comparatively, and whether a man prays alone or in company he ought to feel as if shut in his closet with no witness but God. Pseudo-Chrysostom says the same from the other side: whoever prays to be seen prays in the synagogue so far as his purpose goes, wherever he stands, while he whose mind is fixed on God prays in secret even in the congregation. Henry's rule is practical: secret prayer should be unobserved, undisturbed and unheard.

Clarke opens the word itself, from a root meaning a vow, since a man who prays rightly binds himself to God as by a vow, : prayer is the language of dependence, and the man who does not pray attempts to live independently of God, which was the first curse. He then breaks off to print a hymn of Montgomery's. Pseudo-Chrysostom gives three reasons for praying silently: God is a hearer of the heart and not gained by vehement crying, none but a man and God should be privy to his petitions, and aloud he hinders whoever prays beside him — adding that one should do nothing singular, no crying out, beating of the breast or stretching forth of hands. Cyprian asks how a man can claim God's attention when he does not attend to himself, snatched off by profane imaginings in the act of entreaty; Remigius is content that he alone should know our petitions who knows all hearts; Jerome says the plain sense teaches us to shun vain honour.

On the reward Chrysostom and Calvin collide. Chrysostom presses the wording — he said not shall freely give thee but shall reward thee, so constituting himself your debtor — and explains have received of men who preferred what comes from men. Calvin denies the inference in terms: when Christ promises to reward, he declares plainly that all the reward held out anywhere in Scripture is not paid as a debt but given freely. Clarke's warmth is nearer Chrysostom's: goodness beyond measure to reward prayer itself. Ellicott repeats that the closing adverb is probably an interpolation.
7:
The verb divides the philologists. Barnes and Clarke derive it from Battus, a poet who spun out long weary verses repeating the same sentiment, Clarke citing Suidas; Ellicott takes it from the repeated attempts of a stammerer and would render it do not stutter out your prayers; Robertson calls the etymology uncertain but probably onomatopoetic. For instances they draw on the same stock — the priests of Baal calling from morning until noon at 1 Kings 18:26, the crowd at Ephesus shouting two hours — and Lightfoot the Roman acclamations, let the parricide be dragged, hear us, Caesar, over and over. Lightfoot turns the charge home: the Jews sinned little less, their liturgies heaping up different words importing the same thing, the sin being equal where only the words are multiplied. Clarke adds a Muslim parallel from the Hedayah, which condemns praying by the glory of the heavens and yet comes from a people given to such iteration.

What is forbidden is then carefully bounded. Augustine distinguishes much speaking from enduring fervency: the Lord continued a whole night in prayer, and the brethren in Egypt use frequent but very short prayers, hasty ejaculations, lest fervency be broken off; much speaking is to use in a necessary matter more words than necessary, whereas to entreat much is to importune with enduring warmth, often done better by groans than words. Chrysostom says the prayers are forbidden to be long not in time but in multitude of words, since those who ask should persevere, and Christ does not enjoin a prayer of ten thousand verses. Ellicott grants that the law of Christ does not exclude the iteration of intense emotion, our Lord having prayed thrice in the same words, and leaves open how far the Lord's Prayer or the Kyrie falls under the charge, noting that devout souls find such repetition sustains rather than deadens feeling — though the rosary, he thinks, reproduces the eighteen prayers of the rabbis. Robertson makes the same reservation from Gethsemane. Calvin allows Rome no such latitude, where the efficacy of prayer is thought to lie chiefly in talkativeness and long chanting resounds in the cathedrals as if to soothe the ears of God. Gregory puts it shortest: true prayer is the bitter groans of repentance rather than the repetition of set forms.

Behind the rule stands the harder question, which Jerome states as a heresy of certain philosophers: if God knows before we ask, prayer is needless to one who has such knowledge. His answer is that in prayer we do not instruct but entreat, one thing to inform the ignorant and another to beg of the understanding. The Gloss makes the pagan assumption explicit: the demons could not know what was petitioned until told. Chrysostom says we pray not to teach God our wants but to move him, becoming his friend by importunity. Clarke says prayer is designed not to inform God but to give a man sight of his misery; Wesley, that the chief thing wanting is a fit disposition on our part, which prayer exists to produce. Calvin answers most fully: believers do not pray to inform God, or to urge him as though reluctant, but to arouse themselves to seek him, to exercise faith on his promises, and to relieve their anxieties by pouring them into his bosom — and both truths must stand, that he freely anticipates our wishes and that we obtain by prayer what we ask. Ellicott admits the question can never be answered logically, as with foreknowledge and free will, and offers three partial solutions: that we may see our wants as God sees them, feel how little else weighs beside deliverance from sin, and gain strength in communion with the Eternal. Gill's is plainest: it would be shameful in those who have revelation to imitate men guided only by the dim light of nature.
9:
Whether this is a form or a pattern is settled almost unanimously against liturgical use. Robertson would rather call it the Model Prayer, since Jesus did not use it as a liturgy and there is no evidence he designed a set formula — though there is no harm in one, and good in children learning it. Gill calls it a directory as to brevity, order and matter, noting that the disciples are never found using it and that the other Evangelist does not give it in the selfsame words; Calvin holds that the rule relates not to the words but to the things. Ellicott reads the adverb as simply thus, sanctioning both these words and others framed after the same pattern. Clarke sets it among the Jewish forms; Barnes grants that some petitions were current among the Jews, but never in this combination.

On the first word the emphasis falls on the plural. Cyprian says the teacher of peace and master of unity would not have men pray singly and severally, our prayer being general because we are all one; and it is praying like friends to offer God his own words back, that the Father may recognise the Son's. Clarke reports the Jewish maxim behind it, that none should pray the short prayer — meaning the prayer in the singular. The Gloss adds that my Father belongs to Christ alone, who is Son by nature. Augustine observes that Israel was never taught to call God Father but was set before a Lord over slaves, whereas we have received the Spirit of adoption, and not by desert; the name stirs love, a suppliant spirit, and a confidence of obtaining, since what will he refuse to sons who ask, having first given them to be sons? Chrysostom finds forgiveness, adoption, heirship, brotherhood with the Only-begotten and the gift of the Spirit confessed in that one title; Cyril of Jerusalem marvels that men who had revolted should be given leave to say it. Robertson answers the objection that none may use the word who is not born again: that would mean a sinner cannot pray until he is converted, an absurd contradiction. Ellicott notes that the plural does not forbid my Father in private, but witnesses that the right is nobody's peculiar privilege.

On the clause about heaven Augustine is most original. God is not contained in space, and were he literally in the upper parts of the universe the birds would deserve better than men, having their habitation nearer; he is nigh, not to the tall or to mountain-dwellers, but to the broken in heart. So heaven means the saints, as the sinner is called earth; and this is why we turn east in prayer — not that God is there only, but that the mind may turn to the more excellent nature when the body turns to the more excellent body. Chrysostom says the phrase does not confine God's presence but withdraws the petitioner's thoughts from earth; Pseudo-Chrysostom, that we should blush to bury ourselves in earthly things while our Father is in heaven; Wesley, that he is there eminently but not alone, filling heaven and earth.

Cyprian guards the next petition: we do not ask that God be made holy by our prayers, but that his name be kept holy in us, since those sanctified in baptism need a daily sanctification. Chrysostom reads it as a request about our own lives — make us so to live that all things may glorify thee through us. Barnes puts it as a wish that the name essentially holy be everywhere venerated. Calvin sets out the architecture: six petitions, the first three for God's glory without regard to ourselves and the last three for what our salvation needs, answering to the two tables of the law. Robertson notices that the petitions are aorist imperatives, punctiliar and urgent.
10:
Gill notes that the Jewish form ran let the kingdom of thy Messiah come, and that Christ drops the word Messiah to signify he was already come; Clarke and Barnes quote the rabbinic maxim that a prayer with no mention of the kingdom is no prayer. Ellicott traces the petition to the Messianic hope of Isaiah and Daniel and adds that this kingdom rests not on might but on the acknowledgment of righteousness, ever growing toward a completeness it has never reached. Calvin defines the reign as men voluntarily submitting, brought about partly by the preaching of the word and partly by the secret power of the Spirit.

On the will Augustine offers several readings: as by angels so by men; heaven and earth as spirit and flesh, that the body may not resist the spirit; or as in Christ so in his Church, heaven and earth being husband and wife. He adds that the Pelagians are refuted here, since the Church prays for unbelievers that they may begin to have faith. Cyprian says we ask not that God may do his own will but that we may be enabled to do it, no man being strong by his own strength. Pseudo-Chrysostom takes the closing clause as common to all three foregoing petitions, and admires the middle impersonal wording, since man can do nothing good without God's aid and God works no good in man unless man wills it. Chrysostom hears a prayer for the whole world, and says that before we come to heaven we are bidden make this earth into heaven; Clarke draws from it that salvation is the result of two wills conjoined; Jerome uses the verse against those who affirm daily falls in heaven.

The word rendered daily is the chapter's hardest. Clarke counts upwards of thirty explanations and notes that it occurs in no Greek writer before the Evangelists, Origen saying they coined it; he prefers Theophylact's bread sufficient for our substance. Robertson derives it from the participle for the coming day, and reports that the papyri shed no light until Debrunner found the word in an ancient housekeeping book — so it is not a coinage at all but ordinary trade Greek, a prayer for the next day's needs. Ellicott sets out four senses — enough for the day now coming, for the morrow, for existence, or over and above material substance, the Vulgate's supersubstantialis — grants that the first two are commonly received, and then, against so general a concurrence, declares the last the truest, on the ground of our Lord's own use of bread for what sustains the higher life. Jerome had already rendered it supersubstantial and reports that the Gospel according to the Hebrews has mohar, tomorrow's; Gill cites the Arabic, and Lightfoot paraphrases, provide tomorrow's bread and give it us today. Cyprian and Cyril of Jerusalem read it of the Eucharist, the Holy Bread being appointed for the substance of the soul; Augustine, taking it so, asks how the prayer can be said by the many in the East who do not communicate daily, since after communion we cannot ask for what we have received. Pseudo-Chrysostom never introduces the supersubstantial sense and explains our twice: what God gives he gives through us to others, so that whoever bestows nothing eats another's bread. Gregory puts it shortest, that we call it ours and yet pray it be given, since it is God's to give and becomes ours by receiving. Chrysostom sees Christ descending to the needs of the body and restricting even that by this day; Barnes finds in the plural a standing command for daily family prayer; Calvin explains the order, that though forgiveness far outweighs food our Lord began with the supports of this life so that we might climb by steps; Wesley takes in both the meat that perisheth and the sacramental bread.
12:
Gill notes that nothing is commoner in Jewish writing than to call sins debts; Barnes explains the figure, only a creditor being able to forgive a debtor. Ellicott derives duty and debt from the same word, a duty unfulfilled being a debt unpaid, and takes the plural of sins of omission while trespasses are sins of commission — a distinction he calls convenient but technical. Robertson is blunter: trespasses is a mistranslation made common by the English Prayer Book, right in the argument that follows but wrong in the Model Prayer. Calvin sets the petition first in importance whatever its place in order, sins being a wall hindering our approach and a cloud hiding us from God.

The condition is pressed hard. Cyprian calls it a fixed rule, and adds that a man commanded to pray daily for sins is taught thereby that he sins daily. Augustine finds in it the deathblow of the Pelagians, who say a righteous man may be wholly free from sin in this life; he softens the demand only so far that one who cannot love an enemy still meets the terms if he forgives from the heart the man who asks him. Chrysostom uses the same clause against the Novatians, since bidding the faithful pray for forgiveness shows sin can be remitted after baptism. Pseudo-Chrysostom turns on those who will not use the prayer because they will not forgive: the Father does not readily hear what the Son has not dictated. Cyril of Jerusalem weighs the accounts: offences against us are slight, ours against God need such mercy as his only is. Gregory adds that the good we beg in penitence we should first bestow on a neighbour. Ellicott notes that the better reading has we have forgiven, a completed act before the prayer begins.

The next petition troubles all of them. Barnes says God tempts no man, so the word must mean permitting; Clarke calls it a Hebraism, God being said to do what he only suffers, and derives the noun from a verb meaning to pierce, so sore trial is the sense — whence some fathers added which we cannot bear. Robertson names it a permissive imperative: do not allow us to be led. Ellicott distinguishes trials that test from allurements that entice, takes the former as dominant, and hears the cry of a weakness that fears to fail, echoing let this cup pass from me. Cyril of Jerusalem answers the objection that we are elsewhere told to count it joy when we fall into temptations: to enter into temptation is to be overwhelmed by it, a winter torrent which Judas entered on the love of money and drowned in, while Peter swam through the denial. Calvin insists the two clauses are a single petition, as Augustine judiciously explains. On the last word Ellicott holds that New Testament usage favours the evil one, and Clarke agrees; Robertson answers that the case obscures the gender.

The doxology is disputed as text yet expounded as sense. Clarke reports it rejected by Wetstein, Griesbach and the most eminent critics; Robertson, that it is wanting in the oldest manuscripts and arose when the prayer began to be chanted in public worship. Lightfoot supplies what may lie behind it: in the Temple the people answered not Amen but Blessed be the name of the glory of his kingdom for ever. Those who keep it expound it: Pseudo-Chrysostom maps kingdom, power and glory back onto the three first petitions, and Chrysostom finds it restoring the confidence the mention of our enemy had shaken. Wesley takes the threefold form as answering to Father, Son and Spirit; Jerome calls the Amen its seal. Augustine ends with the largest claim: whatever words we use, if we pray rightly we say nothing not contained here, and he matches petition after petition with a verse of the Psalms.
14:
Augustine notes that of all the petitions the Lord judged this most worthy of further enforcement, the one in which he would have us merciful; and he warns that whoever will not forgive a man seeking it in true sorrow should not suppose himself forgiven. Calvin says the verses only explain why the condition was added: God will not be ready to hear us unless we show ourselves ready to pardon, and those who refuse to forget injuries devote themselves deliberately to destruction and knowingly prevent God from forgiving them. Rabanus ties the promise back to the Amen: the Lord grants whatever is rightly asked by those who do not fail in the annexed condition.

Pseudo-Chrysostom observes the order carefully: it is not said that God will forgive first and we after, for he knows how treacherous the heart is, and that men who have received pardon still withhold it — so we are told to forgive first. Cyprian adds that no excuse will stand in the day of judgment, when a man is judged by his own sentence and dealt with as he dealt. Chrysostom thinks heaven and the Father are named to claim our attention, since nothing so likens a man to God as forgiving one who has injured him, and it would be unmeet for the son of such a Father to live as a slave. Clarke measures the bargain: for a king to forgive a hundred millions of treasons on the single condition that his subjects live peaceably would never be seen among men.

The change of word from the prayer itself is noticed. Robertson says trespasses is no part of the Model Prayer at all, the noun meaning literally a falling to one side, where the other word denotes a positive stepping across. Clarke makes the same contrast tell: what men do against us is only their stumbling, a falling off from duties they owe us, whereas ours are debts to God's justice that we can never discharge — so forgiving should be no great difficulty, especially as we have failed others in the same way. He adds the story of Athenodorus, who advised Augustus to say nothing in anger before repeating the alphabet; a Christian, Clarke says, may repeat the fifth petition instead. Jerome finds an oddity in the word men, since those to whom sins are forgiven are rightly so called. Gill explains why the point is pressed on this audience, the Jews being a people subject to revenge and hardly brought to forgive, and demands forgiveness that is full and from the heart, forgetting as well as forgiving, without upbraiding, and even where the offender neither asks pardon nor appears to repent. Barnes stops short of that: where a man asks forgiveness we are to pardon cordially and for ever, and where he does not we are still to treat him kindly, harbour no malice and be always ready to declare him forgiven when he asks.
16:
Pseudo-Chrysostom joins fasting to prayer as its aid, since a man sunk in self-indulgence cannot have a contrite heart, and gives the rule: better that fasting should show you than that you should show your fasting. Ellicott supplies the history — under the Law only the Day of Atonement was a fixed fast — and adds that the Pharisees fixed the twice-weekly fasts on the second and fifth days, with some notion that Moses went up Sinai on one and came down on the other; our Lord blames neither the principle nor the rule, only the pride that apes humility. Clarke is severe on the word itself: a fast is total abstinence from food, and to abstain from flesh while living on fish is a burlesque of one; nor is there any such thing in Scripture as fasting from sin. Barnes grounds the practice in nature, grief destroying the appetite, so that fasting expresses sorrow before it is a rite.

On the disfigured face Robertson notes a play in the Greek: they conceal their looks in order to appear. Jerome complains that the Latin word here is a translators' blunder, properly said of men exiled beyond a boundary, where the sense wanted is to destroy: the hypocrite destroys his face to feign a sorrow he does not feel. Lightfoot explains the practice literally, faces being disguised with the ashes taken on the head in public fasts — setting Seneca against it, that to hate easy cleanliness and affect nastiness is against nature. Clarke derives the word for their look from a root meaning sour, or from the name of the Scythians, a morose face like a Tartar's. John Chrysostom says we have outdone them, since many neglect to fast yet wear the mask of fasting, excusing it lest they offend the many — an excuse worse than the sin. Augustine warns that display lurks in the dress of mourning as much as in splendour, the more dangerous because it deceives under the name of God's service.

Whether the anointing is to be done is disputed. Lightfoot shows that those who fasted neither anointed nor washed, both forbidden on the Day of Atonement. Jerome takes it from the custom of Palestine, where the head was anointed on festivals, so that we are told to wear the look of gladness when we fast; Barnes reduces it to appearing as on any other day. Calvin calls the language hyperbolical, since Christ does not draw us out of one hypocrisy into another, but requires only that our fasting make no change in our accustomed way of living. Pseudo-Chrysostom agrees, and then reads it spiritually: the face is the conscience and the head Christ, who is anointed when the hungry are fed; we should wash the face but anoint the head, our conscience being foul while Christ our head has done no sin. Augustine says plainly that none would enjoin it literally, and understands the head as the reason and the anointing as joy. The Gloss draws the lesson: behold how everything in the New Testament is not to be taken literally.

What the discipline is for is variously answered. Leo requires it fulfilled not in abstinence from food only but in the cutting off of vices, a work from which the sick are not excluded. Gregory approves the fasting that opens the hand to alms: what you deny yourself, bestow. Gill makes Christ's fast a different thing, lying in abstinence from sin rather than food. Calvin is most guarded: fasting is a doubtful operation and does not stand with prayer among the actions God requires, pleasing him only as directed to something further — subduing the flesh, quickening prayer, testifying repentance. Chrysostom observes that with alms the Lord added to be seen of them but with fasting and prayer added nothing of the sort, because alms cannot be wholly hidden and these can.
19:
Chrysostom explains the transition: having driven off vanity, Christ turns to contempt of riches, since nothing breeds the desire of money like the love of praise — men want tables of silver not for use but to be seen. Wesley marks the same passage from religious to common actions, the love of money as inconsistent with purity of intention as love of praise. Pseudo-Chrysostom counts a threefold destruction awaiting the goods of this life: they are eaten as cloth is, consumed by their owner's luxury, or carried off by strangers — and he calls all men thieves who by unlawful means make another's goods their own. Rabanus divides by kinds of wealth: metals go by rust and clothes by moth, and since precious stones fear neither, a common damage is named that reaches all. Barnes explains the moth historically, treasure among the ancients consisting largely of changes of raiment, as with Achan's goodly Babylonish garment. Ellicott renders it treasure not up your treasures; Robertson notes that the verb for breaking in is literally to dig through, easy in walls of sun-dried brick, so the Greeks called a burglar a mud-digger — Clarke comparing the cobb houses of Cornwall.

Whether anything may be laid up at all Clarke puts as a catechism: treasure may be laid up innocently, first if a man can do it without setting his heart on it, which is almost impossible, and second if there are no widows or destitute persons where he lives. He deals as briskly with objections: a portion belonging to your children is not yours, and a man should keep his principal and give away the product. Calvin charges the covetous with folly rather than crime: they lock their riches in well-secured chests and cannot keep them from moth or thief, when God invites them to riches that never perish. Gill takes the positive command as a direction about earthly goods rather than heavenly hopes — put your treasure into God's hands by communicating liberally to the poor. Calvin guards it, since the command to sell is not to be taken literally, but neither may we be satisfied with bestowing what we can easily spare: liberality should go so far as to lessen the patrimony. Clarke quotes Quesnel, that transmitting goods to heaven by charity is a bill of exchange which cannot fail except through our own fault, and then turns on the idea of merit: a man who thinks to purchase heaven with the meat left at his table has a base and ignorant soul.

The closing proverb is where the weight falls. Chrysostom says that even if none of those losses come, a man loses much by fastening his affections below, and grows unable to think of any lofty thing. Augustine explains the pollution: whatever is mingled with a lower nature is defiled by it, as gold is alloyed by silver though silver is pure in its kind; and by heaven he understands the spiritual firmament, since whatever has a body is earthly. Jerome widens it beyond money to all possessions: the glutton's god is his belly and the lover's his lust, every man serving what he is in bondage to. Hilary observes that the praise of heaven can be carried off by no thief and eaten by no rust of envy. Calvin states the principle sharply: covetous men cannot help breathing some wish for heaven, but wherever men imagine the greatest happiness to lie, there they are confined, so those who want to be happy in the world renounce heaven. Ellicott says the same of the divided mind: men may persuade themselves they will hold a treasure in both places, but one or the other will claim an undivided allegiance. Pseudo-Chrysostom asks why a man should look up to heaven where he has nothing laid up; Barnes concludes that to regulate the heart the treasure must first be right.
22:
Chrysostom says the eye meant is not the outward but the inward, the light being the understanding through which the soul sees God. Pseudo-Chrysostom argues from the words chosen: had the bodily eye been meant he would have said sound or weak, not single and evil. Clarke glosses the adjective as simple and uncompounded, an eye so perfect as to see distinctly and not double, and reports that an evil eye was a Jewish phrase for the covetous man who repines at his neighbour's prosperity. Robertson finds the word used of a dowry repaid pure and simple, its root sense being without folds, like unfolded cloth; a diseased eye may even be cross-eyed, so that we see double, keeping one eye on hoarded treasure and rolling the other proudly up to heaven. Ellicott renders it the lamp of the body and identifies it with conscience, the connection lying on the surface, since singleness of intention preserves us from a double treasure and a divided heart. Barnes keeps the physical illustration: a rope-dancer steadies himself by fixing his eye on the wall, and a man crossing a stream on a log falls when he looks down.

What the eye stands for is then variously answered. Augustine takes it for our purpose, the works being the body, so we should ask not what a man does but with what mind — adding the limit that only acts indifferent in themselves take their colour from the motive, since nobody may say, let us rob the rich that we may give the poor. Hilary makes it the light of the heart, which if single will pour the splendour of its origin back into the flesh at the resurrection. Remigius offers faith, which lightens the goings of the inner man, and the ruler of a church, well called the eye, since if he errs how much more will the people under him. Calvin makes it reason, given to guide affections blind in themselves; men pervert their own judgment until not a spark remains, light turning to darkness when lust overwhelms reason and when men give their minds to craft. Wesley calls it the intention, and observes with what propriety our Lord sets it between worldly desires and worldly cares. Jerome adds that thick eyesight sees the lights multiplied, the single eye single and clear.

The two masters answer an objection. The Gloss supposes a man saying he will do good works from worldly and heavenly motives at once, and finds the saying aimed at him; it distinguishes two kinds of service, freely for love and servilely from fear, so that a man serving contrary masters must hate the one or despise the other. Chrysostom insists the masters must be of contrary orders, since concord makes many one, and thinks two are named to show change is easy: a man given up as the slave of riches may learn that another service is open. Pseudo-Chrysostom ties it back, this being why a spiritual mind can keep the body free from sin. Gill agrees that where orders agree both masters might be served, Barnes that obedience would otherwise be divided. Jerome says mammon is riches in Syriac and marks the wording — not he who has riches but he who is their servant, since the slave of money guards it as a slave while the free man dispenses it as a master. The Gloss and Augustine make mammon the Devil, lord of money not because he can bestow it except as God wills but because by it he deceives men. Augustine notices too that the verb is despise and not hate, since none with a right conscience can hate God, though a man may fail to fear him, presuming on his goodness. John Chrysostom sees the argument built like a physician's, pressing the hearer by both the disease that follows neglect and the health of obedience.
25:
The English of the verse is corrected by nearly everyone. Barnes explains that thought meant anxiety when the Bible was translated, quoting Bacon on a man who died with thought and anguish. Ellicott adds Shakespeare's take thought and die for Caesar, and reconstructs the translators' choice — the phrase was stronger in 1611 than the be not careful of earlier versions, and the changing fortune of words has since made it weaker. He draws the distinction that matters: what is forbidden is not the foresight which provides for the future but the being harassed by its uncertainties, and taking thought in the modern sense is often the best safeguard against taking thought in the older. Robertson notes that the verse is now quoted as an objection to the morality of the Sermon, as though it commanded a reckless neglect of the future; the verb, he adds, comes from a root meaning to divide, because care distracts. Clarke reaches the same root and quotes his old manuscript Bible, be not bysy to your liif.

How far care is then permitted is worked out carefully. Clarke says prudent care is never forbidden, only the solicitude that draws the mind different ways; and he balances it, since to rely so far on providence as not to use the faculties God gave is to tempt him. Gill excludes labour and ordinary forethought from the prohibition and includes only what arises from diffidence and tends to despair. Calvin gives two grounds for condemning immoderate care — that men vex themselves by carrying anxiety further than their calling demands, and that they rely on their own industry until they neglect to call on God — and places lawful care midway between indolent carelessness and the torments by which unbelievers kill themselves. Jerome puts it in a phrase: toil is enjoined and carking forbidden, since in the sweat of our face we earn our bread. He also notes that some manuscripts add nor what ye shall drink, a clause Clarke reports missing from many versions and fathers, and which Griesbach left standing with a mark of doubt. Augustine turns aside to the Euchites, who held that a monk need not work and read the Apostle's rule against the idle as meaning spiritual labour only; against them he proves from Paul's example that bodily work was meant.

The argument itself is from the greater to the less. Barnes counts it the first of four in the paragraph: he who gave life, which is more than meat, and formed the body, which is more than raiment, will not withhold the smaller gift. Ellicott notices the homeliness of the illustrations, the language of one speaking to peasants with simple but pressing wants rather than to the covetous of a higher grade; and the word for life is the one usually rendered soul, taken here in the wider sense. Wesley puts it in a line — if God gives the greater gift, will he deny the smaller? Pseudo-Chrysostom argues from creation: had God not willed that what he made should be preserved he would not have made it, and having made it to be kept by food he must give food as long as he wills it to continue. Chrysostom guards the wording, that the spirit does not need food, being incorporeal, though the soul cannot remain in a body unfed; and he links the verse to what precedes, as answering the man who asks how he is to live once he has given up all. Hilary alone reads it forward, to unbelievers who cavilled about what our bodies would look like at the resurrection and what we should eat in eternal life; he will not have our hope hang on such care. The Gloss compresses the whole into a sentence: be not withdrawn by temporal cares from things eternal.
26:
What the birds are is disputed at once. Hilary suggests that under their name we are exhorted by the example of the unclean spirits, to whom provision is given without trouble of their own, so that are ye not much better than they marks the interval between piety and wickedness. Jerome had no patience with such readings — some, he says, seeking to soar beyond the limits of their fathers, sink into the deep and drown; those who make the birds angels cannot explain how the comparison is put to men at all, and the plain sense must stand. Ellicott prefers birds to fowls, our use having narrowed a word which in Chaucer covered the lark and the linnet, and thinks the words were spoken with a gesture toward the turtle-doves of a Galilean landscape. Barnes lets himself go on them, filling the air in flocks and meeting the morning with their songs, and yet how few die of hunger. Calvin makes unbelief the mother of every care that goes beyond bounds; he notes that Luke has ravens instead, some thinking them named because their parents desert them at birth.

Whether the saying excuses idleness is answered firmly. Augustine turns on those who argue from it that they need not work: why do they not attend to the words that follow, neither gather into barns, and why do they want idle hands with full storehouses? The birds do not grind corn, and if others cook for these men they must at least draw their own water, which birds do not; and laying up nothing for the morrow cannot be kept by men who shut themselves away for days in prayer — will anyone say the holier they grow the less like birds they become? The comparison means only that no servant of God should think his wants unregarded. Clarke and Lightfoot both supply the rabbinic saying behind it: have you ever seen a beast or a fowl with a workshop, or a lion carrying burdens, a fox trading, a wolf selling oil? — they are fed without labour, and the reason man must labour for his bread is sin. Pseudo-Chrysostom turns the argument from less to greater: if birds find food without toil, shall a man not find it who has been given both the knowledge of labour and the hope of a harvest? Robertson makes the same point in a line, that this is no plea for idleness, since even the birds are diligent and the flowers grow.

The last question is what the cubit measures. Barnes observes that terms of length are commonly applied to life, as when the psalmist calls his days a handbreadth, and that the word oftener means age, in which case anxiety cannot lengthen life by an hour. Clarke argues for age outright: place and time are alike quantities, so every tongue borrows the terms of one for the other, and adding a cubit is proverbial for something minute — which suits a small portion of time but not stature, where a cubit would be an extraordinary accession of height. Ellicott allows either but prefers age, men being seldom anxious about their height and often about their length of days, and notes that Luke's parallel calls it the least of things. Robertson dissents, thinking stature probably suits the context best, and adds only that anxiety will help neither kind of growth. Calvin finds a second fault reproved beside distrust: scarcely one man in a hundred does not promise himself what he likes from his own industry, and those who take credit for their prosperity lose sight of God — so Christ reproves pride as well as fear. The Gloss states it plainly, that our own care is not enough even for our being and life; Gill adds that Christ argues now not from the needlessness of anxious care but from its unprofitableness.
28:
Both Chrysostoms ask why the birds are dropped for flowers, when the peacock or the swan lay ready to hand, and answer that the argument had to run two ways at once — the richness of the clothing and the meanness of the thing clothed. That is why the lilies are called grass of the field at the end, and why it is not said that tomorrow they are not, but that they are cast into the oven. Ellicott fills in what was in view: the hillsides of Galilee in spring, with crown imperial, crimson tulips and anemones of every shade, all roughly classed as lilies; and he presses the verb, which asks not a passing glance but study. Robertson agrees it may cover anemones, poppies and irises. Pseudo-Chrysostom notices the division of labour, they toil not spoken for men and neither do they spin for the women.

Whether to read further is the chapter's plainest quarrel. Augustine forbids it outright: these instances are not to be allegorised, and we are not to ask what the birds or lilies denote, since they are examples and nothing more, proving God's care for the greater from his care for the less. Hilary does exactly what Augustine forbids, making the lilies the eminences of the heavenly angels, who neither toil nor spin because they received at their creation a nature that continues as made, and the grass the Gentiles, granted eternal existence only to be handed to the judgment fires. Remigius goes further: the birds are the saints reborn in baptism, the lilies those who pleased God by faith alone, or holy Church for the whiteness of its faith, the grass the unbelievers and the oven eternal damnation — so the sense becomes, if God gives temporal goods to unbelievers, how much more eternal goods to you.

The oven is disputed on other grounds. Wesley calls the still the natural sense, since grass and flowers can hardly be thrown into an oven the day after cutting, nor is it the custom anywhere to heat ovens with them. Clarke says that reading is contrary to the scope of the argument, and reports that easterners heat their ovens with dry straw and stubble to this day. Ellicott supports the oven with detail: the portable earthen vessel the poor baked in, with coarse hay heaped below and round it, the flame short-lived enough to make the crackling of thorns proverbial. Barnes describes the ovens from Niebuhr, the stone-paved pit and the clay-smeared vessel. The Gloss notes that some copies read into the fire.

On Solomon the commentators converge. Clarke, Barnes and Wesley suppose the lily chosen because the robes of eastern kings were white; Ellicott sets against it the tradition that even Solomon's attendants went in purple with gold-dust in their hair, and concludes that the lily shames the king. Jerome puts it rhetorically: what regal purple may vie with flowers, what work of man has the blush of the rose or the white of the lily, and how the Tyrian dye yields to the violet is a thing sight can tell and words cannot. Calvin draws the doctrine that the kindness of God displayed in herbs exceeds all men can accomplish by wealth, and that many who seem to have faith in prosperity tremble at the first danger of poverty. Lightfoot shows the closing phrase common in the Talmudists, who reckoned among the little of faith the man who prays with a loud voice, or who having a morsel in his basket asks what he shall eat tomorrow; the Gloss defines it as the faith not sure even of the least things, and Ellicott observes that the word occurs only in our Lord's teaching and never means unbelief, only a trust too weak. Wesley ends as a naturalist: every microscope in which a flower is viewed gives a lively comment on this text.
31:
Remigius takes the repetition as deliberate, to show how necessary the precept is and to press it deeper. Ellicott notes that what stood before as a general rule is now enforced as the conclusion of an argument, and that a change of tense which English cannot render makes it personal — do not be over-anxious now. Rabanus draws a fine distinction from the wording: it is not seek not food and raiment but what ye shall eat, what ye shall drink, wherewithal ye shall be clothed, which convicts those who use the ordinary fare themselves and require of their companions either more sumptuousness or more austerity. The Gloss finds another needless solicitude condemned, that of laying by more than necessity requires and being intent on it as though despairing of God's goodness. Clarke says the three questions engross the whole attention of men living without God, whose belly and back are a compound god; Wesley calls the precepts kind, their whole substance being, do thyself no harm, and refuses to borrow the anxieties of the morrow to aggravate those of the present day.

The comparison with the Gentiles is handled with varying sharpness. Gill explains that most of them held the soul to perish with the body, so that it is no wonder they sought these things, this being all the happiness they expected — but for those who have revelation to act the same part is absurd and wicked. Pseudo-Chrysostom puts it as a doctrine of Fortune against Providence: believing their lives are directed by chance and not by counsel, they fear and despair as men with none to guide them. Calvin says the same of unbelievers who imagine God unemployed or asleep in heaven, and adds the sting, that those who are anxious about food give his fatherly goodness no more honour than unbelievers do. Ellicott hears pity rather than censure, with a touch of rebuke to national pride: you look down on the heathen and think yourselves God's people, yet wherein do you excel them if you seek only what they seek?

Behind the promise lies the question whether God attends to particulars at all, and Nemesius argues it out. Providence is shown by the continuance of things and the preserving of their order, which no unpresiding power could do; and against those who allow God a general providence while leaving particulars to contingency he offers three possibilities and refuses all of them. Ignorance is alien from a blessed substance, since every wise man knows that if particulars perish the whole perishes. Unwillingness must come either of inactivity or of the meanness of the work; but inactivity arises from pleasure or fear, neither of which may piously be supposed of God, and it is inconsistent that a workman overseeing a machine should leave any part of it unregarded. Augustine meets the objection from number: God did not gain his knowledge at any time but foreknew before all time, and those who say the things are too many to be compassed must equally say he cannot know all numbers, which are infinite — whereas infinity is not beyond the compass of one who is himself infinite, so that all infinity is in an unspeakable way bounded by God, not being incomprehensible to him. Chrysostom prefers the pastoral note: he said not God knoweth but your Father knoweth, to raise their hope, and named the things as necessary precisely so that we should be the less anxious, since a father who denies his son bare necessaries is no father — though for superfluities there is no such confidence. Clarke states the same rule as a balance: not to expect necessaries offends God's goodness, and to expect superfluities is injurious to his wisdom.
33:
What is to be sought first is defined variously. Gill allows two senses, the Gospel and its ministration, or the kingdom of glory for which God makes his people meet here. Ellicott says the context points to the seeking of prayer rather than of act, notes the significance of the kingdom of God where the less personal kingdom of heaven might have stood, and takes the righteousness to be that which, exceeding the Pharisees', must be God's gift and so matter for prayer. Robertson turns the verse against those who find in the Sermon nothing but ethical comment, since here the kingdom and its righteousness are set before food and clothing. Clarke calls it the seventh reason against worldly cares, that the business of salvation ought to engross us entirely — grace being the way to glory and holiness the way to happiness. Calvin makes it an argument against excessive anxiety: it argues a gross neglect of the soul that men born to a better life should be wholly employed about earthly objects, and nothing restrains the wantonness of the flesh like meditation on the life of heaven. The Gloss reads the pronoun strictly — his righteousness, as though to say, ye are made righteous through him and not through yourselves. Wesley adds that whoever seeks this first will soon come to seek it only.

On the promise that follows, Ellicott quotes a saying of our Lord's preserved outside the Gospels by Origen and Clement of Alexandria, ask great things and little things shall be added to you, ask heavenly things and earthly shall be added. Clarke reports the rabbinic version, of a man told by a king to ask what he would, who asked for the king's daughter, knowing that all the dignities of the kingdom went with her; and he quotes Trapp's blunt gloss, that these things are cast in as an overplus, like the paper and pack-thread given with spice, or the inch of measure added to an ell of cloth. Barnes states the plain doctrine, that God has control over all things and will give what he deems best.

The last verse turns from present things to future ones, and the commentators differ over what is forbidden. The Gloss makes it a distinct prohibition, of the fruitless care that proceeds from the fault of men. Jerome shows that tomorrow in Scripture means time future in general, citing Jacob and the Pythoness to Saul, and then concedes what the verse allows: our Lord yields that men should care for things present while forbidding thought for things to come, the uncertain future being left to God. He adds a gloss on the last word — by evil is meant not what is contrary to virtue but toil, affliction and the hardships of life. Chrysostom notices the figure by which the day itself is made to complain of its too heavy cares, a device used by those who speak to a rude populace, and asks whether every day has not burden enough of its own, without adding what belongs to another. Pseudo-Chrysostom reads the two days differently again, taking today for what is needful in this present life and tomorrow for what is superfluous. Gill keeps the distinction practical, that it is lawful to take proper thought for present food and raiment but not to be anxiously concerned for futurity. Barnes turns it on the uncertainty of life: it is wholly uncertain whether you will see that day, and if you do it will bring its own trouble and its own supply, God being the same Father then as today.
